source.title: Beyond Signal Propagation: Is Feature Diversity Necessary in Deep Neural Network Initialization?
source.authors: Yaniv Blumenfeld; Dar Gilboa; Daniel Soudry

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material supplied; no truncation apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how initialization and symmetry-breaking conditions affect training outcomes, using CIFAR classification accuracy and stated training failures rather than measuring training classification error or the initialization-speed/depth measures in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy, not training classification error. It does not test random labels, zero training error, depth without shortcuts, or the claimed normalization comparisons. Its discussion of prior work on residual networks, Fixup, and Delta-Orthogonal initialization is cited background, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether initial feature diversity and symmetry breaking affect trainability and final test accuracy. Those results do not directly test any stated version: V4 concerns initialization-dependent learning speed and trainable depth in plain networks, whereas the extracted rows measure final test accuracy at fixed depth. The reported training delays concern residual ConstNet. Stable signal propagation being insufficient without symmetry breaking does not contradict V4's stated comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that random initialization and initial feature diversity are unnecessary for successful training in their constructions. Ordinary signal propagation must be accompanied by effective symmetry breaking and propagation of symmetry-breaking signals. Hardware noise can suffice for ConstNet, but delays, hardware and precision dependence, and extensive averaging can impair training. They ultimately argue that feature diversity should not be a major initialization concern when small independent perturbations can remove symmetry.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces ConstNet and LeakyNet with identical features at initialization and tests symmetry-breaking mechanisms, rather than reproducing the listed studies' methods. It uses SGD with momentum, cross-entropy, CIFAR tasks, and test accuracy outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Symmetry-breaking mechanism, dropout rate, computation-noise setting, GPU hardware, data type (FP32 versus FP16), and number of averaging versus identity initialized layers affect outcomes. Zero-initialized runs can lag He runs and sometimes remain near 10% accuracy for a random number of epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: With symmetry breaking, almost-zero-initialized residual ConstNet reaches final test accuracy close to random initialization; deterministic training without dropout fails.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random initial feature diversity is unnecessary for successful ConstNet classification when symmetry can break during training.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed LeakyNet depth, replacing identity initializations with averaging initializations reduces final test accuracy despite preserved ordinary signal propagation; symmetry-breaking perturbations are attenuated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preserving ordinary forward and backward signals alone does not guarantee successful training from symmetric features; symmetry-breaking signals must also propagate.

fits_no_version.finding: ConstNet outcomes depend on hardware, precision, dropout and symmetry-breaking speed; zero-initialized runs can spend many epochs near chance accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Successful training from symmetric ConstNet initialization depends on sufficiently rapid symmetry breaking, whose effectiveness varies with computation and dropout.

fits_no_version.finding: In shallow MNIST networks, replicated initial features worsen test error, while 1% initialization noise ameliorates the effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial feature replication can impair shallow-network final accuracy, with small independent perturbations reducing the penalty.

record.problems: Outcomes are mainly test accuracy, not training error; some conditions use only 2 seeds, while LeakyNet Table 2 reports 4 seeds. Zero-initialization performance depends on hardware and symmetry-breaking speed. Table 3 gives no uncertainty estimates and uses 200 epochs, which the authors call sub-optimal. No training-error measurements are supplied.
record.rows_left_out: No separately stated numeric outcome rows omitted. Figure-only correlation curves and seed-distribution plots are not extracted as rows because they do not report the version's training-error measure; text describes those results qualitatively.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error, including corrupted or random labels, and its dependence on capacity, stopping or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU spurious-minimum frequencies and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Depth-dependent training-error degradation, matched shortcut comparisons, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup training without normalization.

Activation-matched initialization effects on plain-network learning speed and trainable depth; variance-matched Gaussian versus orthogonal comparisons; and training at 10,000 layers. Fixed-depth final test accuracy and residual ConstNet delays do not establish these effects.
Recovery above the initial linearized stability limit, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to measured thresholds.
Matched normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup's speed and stability relative to normalized residual networks.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both proposed V4 verdicts: comparable final accuracy does not support its speed/depth comparisons, and failure under deliberately extreme symmetry does not establish their reversal. R7 contains a definite numerical transcription error. Table 3's 3/7 marker interpretation is inferred from the enabled/disabled computation-noise conditions described in the text. Table 4 also contains unextracted CINIC Mixup results, 89.09 ± 0.05% for zero initialization and 89.21 ± 0.01% for i.i.d. initialization; these do not bear on a stated version, so they are not version-bearing missing results.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, zero or near-zero error, random or corrupted labels, and comparisons involving smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes are not reported.
No two-layer teacher-student experiment, spurious-minima frequency, or teacher-student width comparison.
No plain-versus-residual depth sweep or test of deep plain networks. Residual shortcuts are part of ConstNet, but their effect is not compared against an otherwise matched network without shortcuts.

Does not compare activation-matched initializations, Gaussian versus orthogonal weights, or trainable depth. It compares identical-feature initializations with He initialization and examines training outcomes and symmetry breaking.
No learning-rate sweep around a stability threshold, loss-rise and recovery analysis, or sharpness measurement.
No matched batch-normalization versus no-normalization comparison, nor a test of Fixup.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ConstNet with zero initialization, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100/CINIC, and symmetry breaking supplied by non-deterministic computation plus dropout
reader_labels.reason: Zero-initialized ConstNet reaches test accuracies close to i.i.d./He-initialized comparators in R3, R4, R15, R21, R26, R27, and R31–R40.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ConstNet or LeakyNet when symmetry breaking is slow or averaging initialization is used extensively
reader_labels.reason: Some zero-initialized runs have very low accuracy without sufficient symmetry breaking, and LeakyNet accuracy falls as averaging layers increase (R5, R11–R12, R16, R19, R22, R25, R28).
